Introduction
Applying protecting groups is a common strategy in multi-step
syntheses. p-Methoxybenzyl (PMB) ether is one of the most
frequently applied protecting strategies for alcohol protection
attributing to its high chemical stability in the sequential
protection and targeted transformation as well as the easiness
of deprotection under mild conditions (Scheme 1a).[1] On the
other hand, direct transformations of PMB ethers without
deprotection step to other targeted synthetically versatile
functionalities are of high interest for the sake of step-economy.
Known reports are on the direct conversions of such PMB ethers
to aldehydes in a deprotective manner[2] and to the syntheti-
cally less attractive p-methoxy-1-benzoates by the p-methox-
ybenzylic oxygenation[3] under aerobic conditions (Scheme 1b),
however, their direct conversion to carboxylic acids[4] has never
been achieved. Herein, we report a very mild Fe(NO ) · 9H O/
TEMPO-cocatalyzed direct deprotective aerobic oxidation of
PMB ethers to carboxylic acids efficiently (Scheme 1c).
Results and Discussion
We chose the PMB ether of C12 alcohol 1a as the model
substrate. After trial and error, 1 a was successfully converted to
the C12 carboxylic acid 2 a in 94 % NMR yield and interestingly
the PMB part was formed as the aldehyde, 4-methoxybenzalde-
hyde 4a, in 93% NMR yield with 10 mol% each of Fe-
tive deprotection of different benzylic PMB ethers has been
realized. The reaction has been successfully applied to the total
synthesis of natural product, (R)-6-hydroxy-7,9-octadecadiynoic
acid, demonstrating the practicality of the method. Based on
experimental studies, a possible mechanism involving oxygen-
stabilized benzylic cation has been proposed.

highly sterically hindering group such as adamantyl also worked

terminal/non-terminal C� C triple bond, and phenyl group, were

We further scrutinized the substrate scope of the rather
challenging differently substituted benzylic PMB ethers. As
shown in Scheme 3, the electron-withdrawing and potentially
useful groups such as cyano, nitro, trifluoromethyl, or ester
groups are all compatible affording the non-methoxy-substi-
tuted benzoic acids 2 r–u highly selectively in good yields using

the other protected as p-CN (1 w) or p-CF (1 x) benzylic ether,
the PMB ether was highly selectively removed affording 2 w
and 2 x with the p-CN (1w) or p-CF (1x) benzylic ether
untouched due to the much lower reactivity of electron-
withdrawing benzylic ethers under the current aerobic con-
ditions.
In order to demonstrate the practicality of this method, the
natural product (R)-12[5] was synthesized in 8 steps from the
commercially available 1,6-hexanediol (Scheme 4): Aldehyde 8
was obtained from 1,6-hexanediol 6 via protection and
oxidation in 74 % and 76 % yields, respectively. By applying
sequential alkynylation, two consecutive Novozym 435-cata-
lyzed kinetic resolutions,[6] and acetylation, propargylic acetate
(R)-10 was obtained in >99 % ee. The current aerobic oxidation
of (R)-10 successfully afforded (R)-11 in 97% NMR yield under
the standard conditions, which was submitted to next step
without further purification. Finally, the copper-catalyzed cou-
pling of (R)-11 with alkynyl bromide yielded (R)-12 in 88% yield
with 95 % ee.[7]

esters 13[8] and 14[9] were synthesized deliberately and sub-
mitted to the standard conditions. Interestingly no reaction was
observed, excluding the intermediacy of these two esters
(Equations (1) and (2)).

Conclusions
In summary, we have developed an efficient and highly
selective aerobic transformation of PMB ethers affording the
corresponding carboxylic acids under the catalysis of Fe-
(NO ) · 9H O/TEMPO with pure oxygen or air as the green
oxidant. The reaction proceeds under very mild reaction
conditions and allows transformation of a variety of PMB ethers
accomodating many functionalities. No racemization occurred
for PMB ethers of optically active alcohols. Moreover, total
synthesis of natural product (R)-6-hydroxy-7,9-octadecadiynoic
acid (R)-12 has been realized with this reaction as the key step.
Experimental studies indicated a unique mechanism involving
oxygen-stabilized benzylic cation. Further studies are being
actively pursued in our laboratory.
